## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the US tariff on lithium-ion batteries?

Lithium-ion batteries are classified under HTS 8507.60 with a base duty rate of 3.4%. Section 301 tariffs on Chinese-origin lithium-ion batteries add 25%, bringing the effective rate to 28.4% for Chinese imports.

### Are EV batteries subject to additional tariffs? [...] Yes, EV battery cells and packs from China face Section 301 tariffs of 25% on top of the base 3.4% duty. This has accelerated battery production shifts to South Korea, Japan, and domestic US facilities.

### What HTS code is used for batteries?

Batteries fall under HTS 8507 (electric accumulators). Lithium-ion is 8507.60, lead-acid is 8507.10, nickel-metal hydride is 8507.50. Each has different base duty rates ranging from 2.7% to 3.4%.

results.title: HS Code for Batteries (US)
results.content:
Batteries are split between two HTS headings: 8506 covers \\primary\\ (non-rechargeable) batteries (alkaline, lithium primary, manganese dioxide), and 8507 covers \\secondary\\ (rechargeable) batteries: lead-acid, nickel-metal hydride, lithium-ion, and others. Lithium-ion batteries (8507.60) are the most economically significant subheading because they cover laptops, phones, EV traction packs, power tools, and grid storage. General MFN rates range from 2.5% to 3.5% across the heading. Battery [...] The \\lithium-ion EV vs other split\\ at 8507.60.00.10 vs.20 matters for both rate (same 3.4% MFN, but Section 301 stacking differs) and statistical reporting under recent EV-related trade measures.

A practical note: batteries integrated into a finished device (a laptop with a built-in battery, a power tool with a battery pack) generally follow the parent device's classification. Standalone batteries (including OEM replacements and aftermarket packs) classify under 8506 / 8507. [...] 3Skipping the EV-vs-other suffix split at 8507.60.00; EV traction packs (.10) and other lithium-ion (.20) share the same MFN rate but have different Section 301 / IRA exposure.

4Treating batteries integrated into a finished device as standalone batteries; a laptop with a built-in battery is classified as a laptop (8471), not split out under 8507.

The 100% tariff applies to Chinese-made electric vehicles (HS 8703.80) and certain other EV categories, including buses and trucks. The 25% tariff applies to lithium-ion battery cells (HS 8507.60) and battery packs, as well as certain battery components. The 7.5% tariff applies to natural graphite (HS 2504.10) and critical minerals (e.g., cobalt, nickel, lithium) used in battery production. It's important to note that the tariffs are ad valorem, meaning they are calculated on the customs value [...] As of August 2026, the US Section 301 tariffs on Chinese EVs remain at 100%, effectively blocking direct imports. Battery tariffs are 25% on lithium-ion cells and packs, with a 7.5% tariff on graphite and critical minerals. These measures have accelerated reshoring and nearshoring, with US battery manufacturing capacity projected to reach 1,200 GWh by 2026, but costs remain 20-30% higher than Chinese equivalents.

results.title: US Tariffs Impact Electric Vehicle and Battery Markets
results.content:
On May 14, the Biden administration announced the US will impose additional tariffs on $18 billion worth of goods from China, which includes a tariff increase from 25% to 100% on electric vehicles (EVs), and from 7.5% to 25% on lithium-ion (li-ion) batteries for electric vehicles in 2024. [...] For China, considering that North America is the third-largest region for Chinese li-ion battery exports (Asia and Europe are the top two, accounting for a combined 70.8% of export value in 2023), and the United States represents the largest market in North America, this round of tariff increases will undoubtedly directly impact China’s exports of li-ion batteries to the United States in the short term. However, Chinese li-ion battery manufacturers have been actively expanding overseas since [...] \NOTE: exports of li-ion batteries encompass consumer, energy storage, and electric vehicle batteries. The tariffs imposed this time impact li-ion batteries for electric vehicles in 2024, with plans to impose tariffs on non-EV li-ion batteries in 2026.

results.title: A New HS Code for Tesla (and Other EV Makers)
results.content:
Ironically, the electric vehicles these Li-Ion batteries power are yet to be given their own HS code. EVs are covered by the all-purpose “Motor Vehicles – Other” code of HS 8703.90.00. The World Customs Organization has proposed a separate code for EVs as part of the next round of HS revisions in 2017. Look for the US to adopt the revised codes – and for more precise data on trade in EVs – a year earlier, in 2016.

by Descartes Datamyne | Sep 17, 2015 | Imports, Indicators

Yet another sign that electric cars are catching on: A new 10-digit Harmonized Tariff System code has been established for the lithium-ion batteries used to power electrical vehicles: HS 8507.60.0010. Until now, the HS codes did not distinguish between EV batteries and Li-Ion batteries used in consumer electronic devices and power tools. [...] The code became effective in July – and July’s US trade data, the first to capture imports of EV-purposed Li-Ion batteries, was released earlier this month:

results.title: Battery Pack Tariffs: What OEMs Need to Know in 2026
results.content:
3. Does your BMS use components of Chinese origin, and if so, what are the HTS codes and tariff rates?  
    BMS electronics sourced from China carry 25 to 30 percent tariffs that can meaningfully affect smart battery pack pricing.
4. Can you provide full country-of-origin documentation for all materials in my battery pack?  
    Required for FEOC compliance and increasingly expected in defense and medical procurement. [...] Multiple tariff measures took effect simultaneously. A 93.5 percent tariff on Chinese graphite – the primary anode material in virtually all lithium-ion batteries – took effect, representing one of the most significant raw material tariffs in US manufacturing history. A 30 percent baseline tariff on all Chinese goods compounded the impact on battery cells and pack components sourced from China. Steel and copper tariffs of 50 percent added further cost pressure on pack housings, connectors, [...] The first step for any OEM that has not done this recently: audit the entire battery pack bill of materials for tariff exposure by component, by HTS code, and by country of origin. Many OEMs are surprised to find that their “Korean” battery pack contains Chinese graphite, Chinese BMS components, or Chinese-origin copper. A complete tariff audit often reveals that strategic substitution of two or three components can dramatically reduce total tariff exposure without requiring a full redesign.
